newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan contractor becomes latest victim of bubble.
newsitem.headline: Japan contractor becomes latest victim of bubble.

text.p: Japan's troubled construction sector saw its second biggest post-war failure on Friday when a medium-sized contractor sought protection from its creditors after buckling under massive "bubble"-era problem loans.
Tokyo-based Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd said it had filed for court protection from its creditors after abandoning a plan to rebuild its troubled business.
It became the first listed general contractor to go under in Japan's post-war history.
Company president Kunihide Kobayashi told reporters that he decided to seek court protection because the company's business "continued to decline while being unable to reduce debt."
He said that most of the firm's top executives would resign to take responsibility for the failure.
It was the second major failure by a Japanese general contractor in the past four years. Osaka-based Muramoto Construction Co Ltd went under in 1993 with 530 billion yen ($4.69 billion) in debts.

Tokai, listed on the first section of the Tokyo bourse, said it was burdened with debts of 511 billion yen ($4.52 billion). It also tops the list of Japanese builders which have guaranteed huge loans which may not be recoverable.
Tokai's shares were suspended by the Tokyo bourse after they fell on the news and are due to be delisted on October 5.

The news about Tokai renewed market jitters over the fragile health of Japan's construction sector, a major casuality of Japan's bad loan crisis, and prompted sales in shares like Tobishima Corp and Aoki Corp.

"Tokai's application will trigger further sales of shares of construction companies with poor financial profiles," said Hiroyuki Chikusa, an analyst at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.

Japanese government bond prices rose sharply in Tokyo on the perception that Japan's economic recovery was still hampered by bad loan problems and that the central bank would not therefore be able to raise interest rates, traders said.
"That was a buy," said a dealer at a city bank's securities unit. "We had not forgotten the problems at construction companies. But at last, the problems are coming to light."
Japan's construction firms have been struggling to recover from the collapse of Japan's 1980s "bubble" of sky-high asset prices, which left them heavily encumbered with problem loans.
Builders led the bubble-era investment in property and real estate and also guaranteed loans by their real estate units.

The sluggish pace of Japan's economic recovery, coupled with lingering loan woes and a squeeze on public works spending, is putting heavy pressure on builders' earnings and has made any substantial turnarounds doubtful.

Tokai, hit by sluggish property sales and falling land prices, had tried but failed to win necessary financial support from all of its four major banks -- Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Tokai Bank Ltd, the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan and Norinchukin Bank.
Tokai's Kobayashi said a further fall in real estate prices and rising concerns about its financial credibility forced it to abort its initial restructuring plan drafted in 1993.

On June 6, Tokai forecast a parent net loss of 1.6 billion yen ($14.1 million) ($14.1 million) for the year to October 31, 1997, after a scant profit of 175 million yen ($1.54 million) ($1.54 million) the previous year.

The Tokai fallout could cast a shadow over Hokkaido Takushoku Bank, a regional bank now struggling to improve its troubled business through a planned merger with another Hokkaido-based bank and a possible tie-up with Britain's Barclay's Bank.

Hokkaido Takushoku said on Friday it would write off an estimated loss of some 30 billion yen ($265 million) arising from its loans to Tokai by September, but added that this would be offset by profits from a planned sale of shareholdings. ($1=113 yen)
